notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2200.tlg00548.opp-gr: Head2: 'ἐπὶ τῆς οἰκίας ἀριστεύσας' is odd ('hero for the house'); possibly corrupt, rendered loosely. 9.1: '<τῶν> α οἴκου' appears damaged (α likely a footnote mark; probably τῶν οἴκοι 'household affairs'). Later in 9.1 the clause 'ἀλλ’ οὐχ οἱ τοῦτον φιλεῖν λέγοντες' is syntactically awkward and may be corrupt; rendered as the sense suggests. 'δεκάτη' is the tenth-day naming feast for a newborn.

19.2: the text is corrupt at 'ὧς οὐδὲν <ὂν> α ὅ τι οὐ σετε'; rendered as if 'there being nothing you would not [grant]' (e.g. δώσετε or πείσετε), which is a guess. 19.1: the address 'ὦ πάτερ' in a speech to the assembly is odd; it may be corrupt (for e.g. ὦ ἄνδρες), but is translated as it stands. 19.1: 'ὑμᾶς ἐμοὶ δεῖν ἔχειν χάριν, ἀλλ’ ἐμαυτὸν· τοῖς παραταξαμένοις θεοῖς' is punctuated in the edition with a stop after ἐμαυτόν; I have taken the dative with the preceding clause. 'βάραθρον' (the pit) may refer to the Athenian execution pit.

40.1: the text contains an apparent digital artifact ('undefined σ’') between αὐτοῦ and πατέρα; it has been ignored. 49: '03 πάτερ' read as ὦ πάτερ. 51: the edition's punctuation 'πρᾳότερος ἐθέλει· τῶν γερόντων εἶναι δοκεῖν' seems misplaced; translated as one clause, 'he wants to seem gentler than the old men'. 46: Ἥλιε is an oath, 'O Sun'.

52: τοῖς δεσι is corrupt; rendered as if δεσμοῖς ('snares/bonds'). The clause 'what comes from such deeds is stronger under the laws than disowning' is syntactically difficult and rendered loosely. 60: <ἀλλὰ> is an editorial supplement.

In §70, προβεβλημένον is taken as 'put forward as a defence for your safety'. In §72, the stray mark before ἡ δόξα is a printing artefact and is left out. In §74, ὡς πλὴν ἑνός appears to be a slip for πλὴν ἑνός, so ὡς is not rendered.

nodes.text: XLVIII

A man who had two sons disowned one of them. The other, having been the hero of the house's honour, asked as his reward that his brother be taken back. When the father spoke against it, he failed to persuade [them]. He now asks to be disowned himself.

It is not about the matters of the other day that I have stood up again to plead with you, citizens, and with my father, nor to ask for that gift which, before your verdict, I thought was a fine one, and fitting for you to give, for me to receive, and for my father to grant. For I would be absurd if, on matters where in my first speech I could not teach you how just they are, I still held some hope that, if you heard me again, you might perhaps give way.

But since I have said the most terrible thing of all, and have dared an enormous act of daring in reminding my father of reconciliation with his son, I would not ask to receive pardon, not because it is right to be unforgiving and harsh everywhere, but because I see that I deserve punishment rather than pardon. That is why I have stood up to ask, by way of a favour, to pay the penalty for what I asked before. For the one who, in wishing to end his brother's misfortune, grieved his father, ought in justice to share that misfortune.

3. Now it is clear that even if I asked nothing of this kind from you, but stood back from these novelties and spoke of the customary rewards, my father would quickly have done this favour by throwing me out of the house. For those who feign goodwill towards him, but have shown the behaviour of bitter enemies, and on no great pretexts have set the man at war with his own kin, what will they become when they have such an opening, if the one whom the father drives out, [his other son] should bring back home again?

Yet even if it is easy for us to get disowned through our enemies, it is somehow better for it to come about through you. For in that way my father will bear the blame instead of those who provoked him, since schemes contrived in secret are hidden from most people; but this way, as I now ask, by being cast out of the house I free him from reproach, and I myself will bear the blame. And if something unpleasant must happen either to him or to me, it is more fitting that it should fall on me than that my father be put to shame.

As far as the present request is just and reasonable, I am confident I will not fail; but I fear two disadvantages: my age, and my inexperience in speaking. For those who have either reached old age or chosen from the start a life on the speaker's platform, time gives the first the knowledge of many things, and practice gives the second the arts of speaking; but I am as young as you see, and I have lived under arms, so that by as much as I have a surplus of ability to save my country, by so much I fall short of speaking adequately.

Now if I were again announcing something unwelcome to my father, and uttering to him that most painful word, "reconciliation", he would reasonably stand up at once and stop my mouth, having many advantages to win with; but since I am adding something similar to what he has already done, and am fighting alongside my father's desires, I do not know on what grounds he could justly oppose me, and contend against his own imitator.

7. But so that you may not think, judges, that I, who have proved good towards the enemy, have not been so towards my father, and may not attribute the words just spoken to shamelessness or some other vice, hear me briefly, by the gods, as I defend myself. For I trust you will judge that I have either done no wrong or erred unwillingly.

When we were born to our father, judges, and were already of an age to receive education, he sent us both to the trainer and both to the teacher of tactics; he embraced us alike when we came home, and in short gave an equal share of affection to each. Throughout all that time — may I say something good about my brother, father, without your making the praise a charge? — throughout all that time I saw in him, by the gods, not a single one of the things that wrap a young man in disgrace: no mad love affairs, no blows over a courtesan; but we walked as equals, thought the same thoughts, delighted in the same things, and shunned the same things.

While our household affairs were going so well, and we were a model of happiness, Envy fell upon us and overturned everything for which we were envied. For certain men appeared who knew my brother better than I who lived with him, who watched for the old man's fits of anger, as you are accustomed to blame your sons to one another in company, even if they err in the smallest things, which the best of companions declare to be lightness and the common traits of youth, and easy to bear for those not too ill-tempered; but these men, who claimed to love him, instead always magnified whatever happened and fanned the spark, filled the house with so great a war, and so violently enraged our father that he seized and dragged the son he had begotten, whom he had raised, for whom he had held the tenth-day feast, and brought him into court and called him wicked.

And he, stunned by the unexpectedness, by the charges, by his father's shouting and by the bystanders, kept silent, to the point of saying nothing in his own defence out of respect for his father, and chose rather to give up the just claims of his case than to speak out about how he was being slandered. After this, this man here went away having won his fine victory, and my brother [went] into the evils of poverty. And I, lamenting them both, the one for what he had suffered, the other for how he had been deceived, made my laments in secret, judges, for I feared that my tears would become a pretext for disowning [me].

11. This, then, the Good Fortune of the city prevented, preparing through me defeat for our enemies and the situation they are now in; and I did not neglect the practice of civic duties, but I went on grieving, men, and feeling ashamed before my age-mates in the gymnasia, who, pitying my brother for his misfortune, never failed to attack me, standing round me in a circle: "And you, though you go home and eat with your father and share his conversation, did you not stop his anger? Did you not soften his rage? Did you not remove his suspicions? Did you not beg? Did you not weep? Take care you do not seem to approve what was done, putting the inheritance before nature, or rather to have already had some hand in it too."

And yet you remember, father, how often I fell at your knees begging you to cease from your anger, and you pushed me away, and with threats ordered the servants to throw me out. For the slanderers, made more convincing by my brother's very misfortunes, invented things never said anywhere and carried them to this man's ears, not letting his mind settle. What then was left? To grieve at what had been done, yes, but to keep quiet perforce, and to call on the gods as reconcilers.

While we were in this state, an enemy invasion was announced. The country districts were being plundered, the danger was approaching the wall, running and fear and confusion gripped everything, and one had to seize arms and run and offer one's body for the fatherland.

Now I give the credit for the good things that befell us, and for the blow to the enemy, to the skill of the generals, to the common zeal, and above all to the turn of Fortune; but these people, as you see, all reckon the rout to my account, and each at home tells his family of my deeds, and they have filled the marketplace with talk about me, and now they have come to rejoice with me in the honour.

For me, as long as I hoped to rescue my brother from his troubles, the narration of my daring deeds was perhaps a fine thing: how, while still going out, I was full of fury and chafed at the delay, and when I saw the enemy I fell on them like a thunderbolt, casting off all concern about suffering anything and looking to the glory of action; and how I broke the phalanx, and my sword was constantly at work, and some were driven off and others taken alive, and the plain was full of corpses and flight, and for the soldiers encouragement came not from words but from my deeds.

These things, judges, I both rejoiced in doing and delighted in narrating, as long as I believed them to be noble and not unequal to words; but now I would say only this much: that of all the citizens it is I whom the enemy curse most.

17. Consider, then, what sort of man I became after the victory, and test my character by the reward. For when we had given back the dead under truce, and the trophy stood, and I was conspicuous, praised and applauded, my fellow demesmen, my fellow tribesmen, my fellow students, and all who knew of the grief I felt for my unfortunate brother came up to me and said: 'Now what you have long longed for has come. Now is the time to ward off your brother's misfortune, to give him back his home, and to free your father from the reputation that his bitter judgement brought him.

It is likely that he, out of respect for your excellence, will become somewhat gentler towards that one too. You must speak to the people, bring about the reconciliation through them, and along with the other things the law allows you to receive, request this too. You are certainly worth a great deal to everyone, and you have from your valour the right to make a just request.'

After this, then, there was an assembly, and when I was called I came forward, a man downcast at his reward for valour, for the misfortune of my house took away the cheerfulness my successes would have brought; and after mentioning the battle and saying that you ought not to feel gratitude to me, but I myself to the gods who fought alongside us, 'Nevertheless,' I said, 'since you bid me make a request, the customary things, father, through which those who receive them gain wealth and distinction, such as plethra of planted land, or talents of silver, or meals in the prytaneum, or a bronze statue, these splendid things,' I said, 'I am not yet in a fit state for; but give me a reward.'

20. And overcome by tears I fell silent; but when you bade me speak and take courage, as there was nothing you would not [grant], I spoke of the Fury of our house, which tore apart what nature had joined, of my brother's misfortune, of my father's anger, of how we are ill spoken of, of how we are made a tragedy everywhere; and finally, instead of a statue, I asked for this much: to see my brother at home. At this you all broke into an uproar, thinking the character of the request finer than the deed of valour.

And one could hear some on this side calling me the good man, others on that side the best of men, and from everywhere, in short, some word or other tending to praise. But indeed, judges, the admiration lasted only as long as my father's silence; when he opened his mouth and uttered something and knitted his brow, everything had been ruined: what had till then been fine had been shown up as base, you had changed your minds, I myself seemed to be out of my wits, and I was blamed for the very things for which I had been gaining esteem.

So great an advantage in a contest, judges, is the title of father. All those great and wonderful names were gone: the guardian of the house, the terror of the enemy, the saviour of the city, the protector of families, the one more useful than the wall, the one who gave cheer in place of trembling; and the victory celebrations became laughable, petty and nonsense.

Since, then, I have troubled you, grieved my father, and let fall words worthy of silence, I have found, judges, another reward through which I hope to gladden the old man. The misfortune I could not lift from my brother, I ask to share, and to be deprived of the house along with him.

24. 'This is a punishment, not a reward,' someone will say, and he will list the honours with which you repay the dangers of the bravest, saying it is madness to flee these and willingly step into so great an evil. But I, if violent grief unseats the reason, admit that I am mad, having come to such a desire. For who has been, or is now, more wretched than I?

And I pass over the rest, but this present moment itself, how much misfortune it holds! The people are at sacrifices and festivities, and women and children and slaves enjoy their safety with pleasure, but only the man responsible for these things is in lamentation, in dirges, because [my brother] is exiled from his father's hearth. I am a citizen of the victors, but I groan with the vanquished. For others the wearing of garlands comes from my zeal, but for me, instead of this, from the people comes weeping. I had the strength to free the city from its fears, but I did not have the power to free my brother from disowning; and what I expected to obtain as an addition, I have not been able to receive even on its own. And worst of all, I disgraced the victory with a wicked request, and though I had saved the laws I was led into [asking] a cruel and lawless reward.

Do not be surprised, then, if by such a concourse of evils I have been driven out of my reason, and, grieving at some things and ashamed at others, I am not altogether in my right mind. But even if someone thinks I am very much not myself, I can at least see this much: the things that bring a man distinction are received by those who fare well, and they obtain what is fitting for those whom the occasion suits, and blame is absent; but if someone in difficulty, seeing his family in the direst straits and unable to help them, thinks of honour and lays claim to distinction, him we both hate and blame and consider hateful to the gods. For what is untimely is blamed everywhere.

And now my unfortunate brother, my opposing father, and the people persuaded by him do not allow this to be the time for these things. Do you want me to stand in bronze in the marketplace when my brother does not even dare to appear in the marketplace? To dine in the prytaneum when he has been deprived of the table at home? To receive talents while he is begging? To obtain proclamation while he has been disowned by proclamation? Do not, by Zeus, do not make me wicked towards nature, nor show me neglectful of her laws, which have prescribed that kin should rejoice in the same things and grieve at the same things. And of all kinship a brother is the most honoured.

Come, if he had died recently, and the victory had coincided with his death, and the people were sitting to decide on a reward, do you think I would accept these solemn things, the garland, the statue, and the rest, and would not rather ask as a favour to receive some time for mourning? Now he has not died, but, what is much heavier than death, he goes about without honour, or rather he hides. What, then, does the occasion advise me to request? To share his dishonour with him, and not to luxuriate amid the misfortunes of brothers.

Every reward is judged by the pleasure of the one who receives it, and what is painful, even if it is otherwise among fine things, counts as punishment. For instance, who would not pray to receive a garland for goodwill towards the people? But if you raise a man sitting in mourning and bring him to the assembly to honour him with a proclamation, you have punished him with the honour. And we resent tyrants for this reason, that they often throw the established rule in these matters into confusion.

I too am mourning a brother driven out, and Fortune takes the garland from my head. For if one of my companions, whom the sharing of exercises binds in goodwill, had fallen into such an evil, do you think I would bear my acquaintance's misfortune moderately, or approach the fruits of valour amid my familiars' ill fortune? But the one for whom I was just now supplicating is my brother, father. That is one just claim. A fellow student. That is a second. One who respected me throughout. That is a third. For I will not call bold, father, one whom I have known to be reasonable.

It would have been better, then, for him to share in my good fortune; but since Envy struck against it, a second gain for me is this very thing, to share in his evils. Different men among those who have won the prize for valour, judges, admire and long to receive different things: one a captive woman in her bloom, another gold from the spoils themselves, another possessions and farmlands, another things that bring glory rather than profit. I too longed to see, through you, my family at peace. I seemed to talk nonsense; I have been defeated in argument. I will go on to another reward, fitting for one who has failed of that one.

32. And let no one think I am ignorant of the misery that awaits the one cast out of his house: hunger, going unwashed, sleeplessness, humiliation, dejection, lack of clothing, continual lamentation. For the teacher of these things is close at hand, and I know precisely everything about those who have come to this, and I need not learn from you that it is more bearable to fall into the pit than to endure this fortune. I have my instructor at home. But if I were ignorant of the terrors of expulsion and did not know the matter better than anyone else, I would not have made it the greatest thing of all to give my brother back his home.

You think that I am hurrying towards disowning as towards something good, but that is not how it is. How could it be? I know every terror of it, yet all the same I long for the misfortune. Grant me this favour, since you were prevented from granting the earlier one. You see, judges, those who do not think it right to live after the greatest misfortunes. They are not ignorant of how terrible death is, for they are among those who have often prayed for their safety; yet they long to die, and they consider the one who opposes them an enemy, and the one who puts the sword in their hand a benefactor. For whoever helps men who want something, whatever it is, to get what they desire is their friend.

And now I, through grief, have come to desire what is strange, and to those who help me here I will owe a gratitude remembered for ever. If any blame should later attach to the prize, let it be mine, who wished to receive it, and not that of those who gave it, who attended to the pleasure of the one asking for the reward more than they considered the harm.

Before now I have seen some who, when their brothers were ill, willingly shut themselves off from food and, as far as they could, shared in their hardships, and from this gained the best reputation, or rather, if the truth must be told, escaped the worse one. For the man who is not good to his family, what would he be towards the people and the city? This is what the reward means to show all mankind in my case too: that I do not neglect to be good, and that I have not learned only to frighten enemies, but also to share the pain of brothers in misfortune.

So if robbers had overpowered us and kept him in fetters but made me their table companion, and oppressed him but let me live in luxury, and inflicted every unpleasantness on him but provided me with every pleasure, I would have begged them not to punish me with delights or torment me by pampering me, but, if they were making him suffer, to bind me too and give me as a gift a share in the pains.

And now, father, I address the same words to you: you have cast out my brother, but not yet me. You have handed him over to poverty, but I live in abundance. If there is no truce between you and him, set me too within the war. Do not prevent the people from giving a reward through which I shall be shown to honour nature.

38. 'But he,' he says, 'turned out wicked and deserved to suffer this.' But as for me, if I had stood up to attack the expulsion and used words like these: 'Citizens, slander has destroyed my brother for me. He has paid the penalty for wrongs he did not commit. My father is quick-tempered. He expects his sons to be without fault, an impossible thing. And shouting and uproar cast darkness over what was just. The young man is unfortunate, but in no way wicked'; if, in short, my present effort were aimed at a defence, then too accusation would not be out of place. But if I let the charges stand, and count it sweeter to fare badly with him than to enjoy good things alone, what further need is there of the accusations?

You have shown his wickedness, father. You persuaded a humane people to dishonour Pity. I am not so foolish as to seek still a defence of wickedness so great and so lately condemned. For what did I not say of all that could be said? Did I not say that youth is very easily led astray, and that those who have not yet gained understanding with time go wrong? That never erring is reserved for the gods? Did I not say what I have often heard from you, that the law's intent is to inspire fear, and that it wants the young to dread expulsion so as to behave sensibly, but that it is not right for them to be driven out and wander homeless when they have a home, for trivial faults? For if they were great, why did he not kill him?

And indeed I asked my father whether he had passed through his youth without fault, and when he could not say so, I asked him to imitate his own father towards us; but in saying this I was declaiming in vain, swamped by the name of father.

What then do I say? That neither should I, the defeated, be allowed to bring up the defence, nor he, the victor, abuse. For the vote has ended the need for both, and my brother's having been wicked has nothing to do with my wish now to be cast out.

42. And indeed, the more he makes him out in his speech to be vile, the more he should take thought for my virtue, so that the father may not be wholly unfortunate, but may have one son who is wicked and another who is not. If, then, I am cast out and my brother takes me as a willing partner in his misery, I shall be called good, just, respectful of nature, everything that is finest, and through me you, the parent, will be envied. But if (may it not happen, nor be!) I choose my own interest and pass over his, I shall be called wicked, cruel, impious, one who knows neither gods nor retribution, everything that is worst, and through me the father will again be in disgrace.

So do not tolerate a double pain coming upon you, but console the earlier disowning with a disowning, the earlier one with the present one, the one from you with the one from me. For the one was a sign of your son's wickedness, the other of your son's nobility.

You must consider it more bearable to be disgraced in your sons by half than completely; or you will at once see the city full of such words as these: 'Quite so. For he is not a wholly good champion who drove the enemy from the land but did not bring his brother back home. He snatched good luck in arms; he did not display virtue. If he practised virtue, he would certainly have added to the trophy the setting right of his family.'

45. And the request, father, and seeming to be defeated, does that carry little blame? For it is easy to find an argument against that too: 'The reward was a fiction and a trick, humane words, but the intent was not so. A seemly show, not the work of truth. He mocked his wretched brother but did not rescue him from his evils. He brought his misfortune out into public view but did not try to remove it. He discharged a formality before the many, he dissembled, but he is working to make the hatred stand immortal. For did he not himself contrive the first steps too? Was it not through his malice that his brother was driven out and nature was wronged by slanders?

If this had befallen from some other source and he was not pleased with the misfortune, he would quickly have ended the trouble with supplications, entreaties, pleas, laments, tears, always present, keeping company, living alongside [his father]. It would also have counted for much towards reconciliation to call his brother to mind with a groan over the wine. But he did none of these things, or he would certainly have moved the parent from his anger. For he would surely not have been fiercer than wild beasts, or hated his son more than the enemy, with whom he has often made truce together with us when they came at us in arms, O Sun, and had destroyed many of the citizens and were eager to raze the city.

For this is humane and safe, never to go beyond measure. You have defeated enemies: make a truce. You have taught your son sense by casting him out: take him back. But the august champion was seen to be good in his request, but base in not being angry when he failed, and by bearing calmly the failure to persuade he wiped out the praise for what he had proposed.
But what should he have done? Fled so pitiless a father, hated unceasing bitterness, changed sides to his unfortunate brother, considered poverty with him sweeter than his father's wealth.'

49. So that I may not be caught in such suspicions, I indict myself for expulsion. And you too will gain, father, by my being the one who writes this. In what way have I grieved you by not hating my brother, and do I owe you a penalty for my goodwill towards him?

I see that those who set you at war with him are still powerful with you even now. I know, then, that they will apply the same device, and lead you astray all the more easily since you have grown used to disowning lightly and daring to shout in court: 'I make a stranger of the one I begot.' You will not hold out against these sophists, father, not even if you very much wish to respect my valour.

51. Do you want me to tell you in advance the very words of these charlatans? 'You had an enemy at home and did not know it. You were raising your son against yourself. Our noble fellow is a father-beater. He did not lay his hands on you, but he did not let up pressing you with words. He wants to seem gentler than the old men. Let him go to the one he values more. Let him pay the penalty for his insolence. Show that you are angry, that what you have heard is not fitting.'

With such [words] they will at once go off, I know, having caught you in their snares, and nothing will stand in the way: not the trophy, not the applause, not the dignity of valour, nor the fact that what comes from such deeds is stronger under the laws than disowning itself (for I have learned something of this sort). For anger, whenever it boils over, thrusts reasoning aside and is carried wherever it happens to go.

53. Consider, then, how I love you, even though you grieve me. I offer you a way to exact punishment while escaping the shame. For my being thrown out of the house by my own speech punishes [me] by my having no share in my father's property, and it gives you, while you stay silent, what you desire without blame.

54. Come: if you wished to drown me, and I anticipated you and threw myself into the sea, would I not be doing you a kindness by choking to death and freeing you from the pollution? And if you would gladly have killed me with a sword, and I, perceiving this, drove the iron into myself while you were delaying, would I not have done you a favour by dying and keeping you clean of the murder?

55. With the same intention I now wish to be disowned. Let a charge of madness fall on me rather than one of impiety on my father; let someone say that the young man is deranged rather than that the old man is out of his mind. Take your penalty, father, take it for great offences. I reminded you of humanity, I reminded you of the name of brother, I blamed anger, I praised forgiveness. Somewhere in my speech to the people was the word 'reconciliation', and I invoked Pity. I owe a penalty for decent words. Disown me, throw me out, do not change your ways.

56. 'But, by Zeus, it is not expedient for the hero to live in grief and for this reason neglect his training for war and provide pleasure to the enemy. For it is clear that his troubles are a festival for his opponents.' What are you saying? Are you afraid that, falling into grief, I will neglect my arms? As if my affairs were now in cheerfulness, songs and laughter? Judge my despondency, man, by my face. With it I live, through it I am ruined. My whole life is grief to me.

57. If I go into the agora, I weep as I talk to my acquaintances about him. If I go home, I mourn as I see the household mutilated. If I come to the wrestling-school, I lament as I see my brother cast aside. Every moment and place is an occasion for tears: house, alleys, gymnasia, gatherings, table, sleep. For already even in my dreams, thinking I have him at home, I leap up for joy, and learning the deception I wait for day amid lamentations. As witness of my many tears I have this very father, who has often been angry at them.

58. So the very thing you fear about the disowning, that by casting me into despondency you will make me worse, already troubles me now. For the only hopes I had of undoing my brother's misfortune have proved vain, and valour did not have the strength to defeat the disowning.

59. Then what pleasure is left to me for the future? Do you think good cheer lies in plenty of food, a soft bed and splendid vessels? That is not how it is. How could it be? Rather, when cheer leads the way, these things too have some charm for some people, but a lavish table does not lighten strong grief; quite the opposite, mourners take pleasure in meaner things, and if you lead them into luxury, you have crushed them further.

60. Do not suppose, then, that my father's house will be a sufficient encouragement to training for one so stricken, and a strengthening of that strength [of mine], <but rather> its undoing. Could I persuade [you] by saying what I will be like, thrown out of the house or staying? Now, at any rate, it is a danger for me to be with my brother, to give him my right hand and to talk with him. And just as those who do the most terrible deeds have their safety in escaping notice, so we too barely and secretly dare this.

61. Many are the spies — drinking companions, flatterers, slaves — and they run straight to him and stir him up, gratifying him by doing harm. And from this our dinner becomes accusations and indictments, and the feast comes with threats. Again, another, seeing those men in favour, keeps watch and toils at the hunt, and often reports both what he saw and what he did not see. My father is in other respects not wicked to us, but he does not know how to disbelieve. Whoever, then, fears the grief to come as a harm to come to the city in war, let him consider the present grief too, and perhaps he will find it greater.

62. 'But it is terrible to gladden the enemy.' Is what has now been done not enough to gladden them? When the assembly rises, many will run to them announcing my disgrace. Do you not think they will open the temples and sacrifice as for trophies, and lighten their grief over their fallen by the insults I have suffered over my request?

63. For what greater thing could they seek? A man who turned their boldness into fear, who showed them suffering what they threatened to do, who slaughtered some and exposed others as cowards, who changed their desire for others' goods into caution for their own, who bereaved some of children, some of parents, and many women of husbands; a man who adorned the town with the spoils taken from them, who drove off the dangers approaching, who preserved temples, sacred things, money, persons, the tombs, the city, the countryside, and granted [them] to sing paeans and be crowned instead of trembling; who first fell upon the midst of the hoplites, scorning his own safety and longing for vengeance — this man, the cause of so many goods, called by the people to a reward, asking not wealth for himself nor what has often profited those who received it and grieved those who gave it, but claiming as his prize to reconcile a father with his son, was shamefully and dishonourably gagged, and was all but held a father-beater and liable to penalty under the laws.

64. Small things, are they not? Are these not for the pleasure of our opponents, and will they not instil hopes in them again? Do not, then, seek how not to give them what you have already given, nor begrudge those whom you voted to console the pleasure to come; but grant, men, grant me the second favour, since you found the first greater than [my] valour. Throw me out of my father's house, since you could not bring my brother back.

65. Why do you hesitate? Do I wish to receive something? The favour is deprivation of what I have. Just now, gratifying my father, you wronged the man who won the prize for valour; now you will vote something pleasing to both. Make me homeless, a thing most pleasant to me; rid him of a son, a thing customary for my father.

66. But if, sparing me, you do not grant this, you have discredited your former judgement. For you will admit that you insulted one you know to be useful. All you old men who did not become childless thanks to us, all who did not leave young children orphans, all who did not see your wives dragged off to outrage, all who are securely wealthy, all for whom I guarded possessions and houses, give me this favour in return. Throw me out of my father's house.

67. Say nothing in reply to this, father, and do not stir up your cleverness again. No more of those former things, speeches on nature and kinship and gods of birth and child-rearing, and humanity and forgiveness and the slips of youth. Rather, come forward and follow the decree, keep the law you laid down, utter the same words again. Now you need no clerk to read the law; you know the syllables of disowning.

68. Do not feel shame before my valour, nor the captives I took, nor the multitude of the dead. You persuaded even the people to belittle what until then they admired. Live alone in the house, be rid of my tears. I cannot, living with you, forget my unhappy brother. You begot me good, father, merciful, compassionate, feeling something at the fortunes of my kin. Accuse nature. So-and-so is violent, another cruel, another hard; I am humane. One cannot fight nature.

69. I owe you thanks for many things: birth, upbringing, education. I repay you by fleeing the house. I know what pleases you, father. By the recent disowning you taught me my present defence. This, then, I ask, and this I consider a fine and fitting reward for me. There is no danger that the sycophants will find you alone and overrun you. For I will keep away from the house, but I will not depart from goodwill, since it is from goodwill towards you that I ask to receive even this.

70. You will see this wicked brother too, along with me, set forth as a bulwark for your safety. I judge this from the time since the disowning, in which, though so greatly oppressed, he has uttered nothing hurtful against his father, but continues to accept the blame and to find fault with himself rather than with those who slander and accuse him. He admires his father and does not withhold from him what is due, but he reproaches his own fortune and is eager to wipe out his disgrace by noble deeds.

I will soon show him to you a good soldier, and you will be called the father of two heroes. Many men, many times, after a blameworthy youth, on coming to the proper age, have been admired for their virtues, and, changing their ways like a costume in a play, some have appeared brave instead of cowardly, others self-controlled instead of licentious, others reasonable instead of rash, others industrious instead of idle, others moderate instead of wanton; and casting off the things for which they were formerly reproached, they ended up as good men and as the greatest benefactors of the city by what they displayed on its behalf. For the matter of valour, even if at the moment it is thought trivial, a little later is recognised for how great it is.

The applause will console my want, the memory of the battle my need, glory my poverty. We will have no house, but we will camp near the trophy. This is my hearth, this my refuge, this my encouragement for the future. The enemy will be content to keep quiet, I know the blow they suffered; but if, as human affairs go, they should recover their old strength, you will find many who will imitate me.

To them I will speak in your presence: men who have courage in the face of dangers and goodwill towards your homeland, disregard for the body and love of honour, let none of you, condemning the people for ingratitude, unwillingly grow faint-hearted, nor, looking at my disgrace, hang back. I write this against myself. I consider the misfortune a reward. I desire poverty. Consider this my madness, not the city's lack of feeling. I flee the house in which I could not show my brother. But you, be men, and do not be troubled by my example.

74. I praise everything about the disowning except one thing: it will make the enemy more cheerful. But you, father, even if you are later hated by the citizens, will be well thought of among the enemy. Feast, then, and drink with pleasure, and rear flatterers as your heirs in place of your sons.
